This discovery was significant because it provided the first clinical evidence that uniparental disomy could lead to a genetic disorder by unmasking recessive mutations or affecting imprinting, thereby contributing to our understanding of genetic mechanisms underlying various diseases.

In that case, two copies of maternal chromosome 7 were present, meaning that the patient had no paternal copy of chromosome 7. This resulted in uniparental disomy for chromosome 7, which can lead to clinical manifestations due to the absence of the paternal genetic contribution.
